 Harris County judge who berated IT worker in viral video is publicly warned by state commission
 Milliron, a Republican, was first elected to the 215th District Court in Nov. 2024 by a margin of just over 300 votes. His current term ends in December 2028.
 Kyle McClenagan | Posted on November 17, 2026, 12:25 PM 
 Share
 Facebook 
 Twitter/X 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Kyle McClenagan/HPM A plaque outside Judge Nathan Milliron’s courtroom at the Harris County civil Courthouse. April 9, 2026. 
 A Harris County judge who berated a county IT employee in a viral video earlier this year has been publicly warned by the Texas State Commission on Judicial Conduct. 
 The commission, which reviews complaints filed against judges, found that Judge Nathan Milliron of Harris County's 215th District Civil Court failed to be "patient, dignified and courteous towards" county employees and others across multiple instances. The commission released its findings in a public warning to Milliron earlier this month. 
 According to the commission, a public warning does not carry any tangible consequences other than being submitted as public record. 
 Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox. 
 Milliron received public scrutiny in March when a courtroom video of Milliron being impolite to an IT employee went viral. 
 “Don’t joke around,” Milliron said in the video. “Get out of my courtroom … Find his supervisor, Jesus Christ, I’m sick and tired of this bull…” 
 According to the committee's public warning, Milliron accused the IT worker — whose identity has not been released — of having a "cavalier attitude towards the court" and claimed the employee called him an "a*****e." 
 "I could have done better, I do own this," Milliron said in response to the Commission. "I never expected someone from the County's staff to call me an a*****e in open court in front of a courtroom full of people before my docket. I was caught off guard." 
 Milliron, a Republican, was first elected to the 215th District Court in Nov. 2024 by a margin of just over 300 votes. His current term ends in December 2028. 
 In a statement to Houston Public Media, Milliron said he had no comment other than he respects the Commission's public warning and looks "forward to serving the good people of Harris County." 
 The commission said Milliron also "acknowledged there was nothing in the IT worker video to support this contention." 
 The viral incident gained additional traction when well-known Houston attorney James Stafford emailed Milliron about the viral clip and asked him to apologize to the county IT employee. In response, Milliron ordered Stafford to appear in his courtroom and accused him of ex parte communication — a one-sided communication between a judge and only one party in a legal proceeding. 
 This email exchange then spilled over into the public when the Harris County Criminal Lawyers Association defended Stafford and condemned Milliron's actions. 
 Ultimately, Stafford did not appear in Milliron's courtroom , and instead a group of attorneys appeared in support of Stafford. 
 In response to this incident, Milliron told the commission he "mistakenly believed Stafford had ‘an active matter in the 215th District Court and [he] perceived his message as an attempt at an ex parte communication.'" 
 The commission's public warning also referenced two other incidents in which it found Milliron had failed to act accordingly. 
 One incident occurred in March when Milliron had an email exchange with the Harris County District Clerk's Office's Civil Court Supervisor in which he complained about the staffing of his court. 
 In one of the email exchanges included in the commission's warning, Milliron wrote: "I'm the District Judge, and you are absolutely a subordinate." 
 In another email to the same county employee Millrion wrote: "THIS IS NO LONGER AN ASK. GET ME A CLERK THAT RESPONDS TO ME and does the job." In an excerpt from a text message included in the commission's warning, Milliron also told a clerk that: "[a county employee] can kiss my a–." 
 Milliron told the commission that the civil court supervisor had thin skin. 
 "Having come from private practice, I was used to an environment where people actually did their jobs in a timely fashion and, if not, there were repercussions," Milliron said. 
 The last incident referenced in the commission's warning related to a March 3 hearing in which Milliron directed his bailiff to remove an attorney from his courtroom during an apparent argument. Milliron told the commission he did not remember the incident specifically but said he had to maintain order in the courtroom. 
 "When the hearing ended, the argument(s) should have ended also," Milliron told the commission. "I believe it wholly unfair to complain about or punish a judge for doing his job." 
 The Harris County Criminal Lawyers Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the committee's public warning against Milliron.
